title: Physics-Informed Graph Neural Networks for Surface Code Decoding via Discrete Exterior Calculus
authors: P. E. Trevisanutto, S. Dhanpal, S. Basak, L. Petit, J. Thiyagalingam
abstract: We introduce a physics-informed graph neural network decoder for the surface code. A discrete Poisson equation on the syndrome graph acts as a hard inductive bias on which a graph encoder learns syndrome-adaptive edge weights. A differentiable solver returns the node potentials and the associated edge current. Our central observation is that the logical-error signal is not carried by any part of that current, but by how the syndrome sits relative to the two code boundaries. We place a sink on each of the two boundaries linked by the logical operator and read the difference of the currents they drain. We prove that this single number is a topological pairing: it weighs each excited detector by a smooth coordinate that runs from +1 on one boundary to -1 on the other, and sums the votes. The coordinate is fixed by both the code topology and the learned metric, generating an exact and free-parameter readout. On the rotated surface code under circuit-level depolarising noise, this one topological scalar matches the best full-field readout. That parity is itself the result: for one logical qubit the logical signal is one-dimensional, so projecting onto it discards nothing. At larger code distance the picture strengthens indicating that isolating the pairing helps more as the field grows larger and sparser.
summary: The paper introduces a novel physics-informed GNN decoder for surface code quantum error correction. It bypasses limitations of traditional decoders by interpreting the logical error signal not as total current, but as a topological pairing measured by the difference between currents drained at two distinct code boundaries. This approach proves highly effective and scalable to larger code distances.
main_problem: Developing a robust decoder for quantum error correction (QEC), specifically for the surface code, that overcomes limitations of traditional methods like Minimum-Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) when noise models are complex.
main_result: The authors propose and demonstrate that measuring the difference in currents drained at two boundary sinks yields a topological pairing signal ($\Delta J$) that accurately matches the best full-field readout for surface codes under circuit-level depolarizing noise.
method: They employ a physics-informed Graph Neural Network (GNN) decoder, embedding a discrete Poisson equation as an inductive bias to calculate edge currents. The key is reading the logical signal from the difference between two boundary sink currents rather than the total current.
model_or_system: The system modeled is the surface code used to encode one logical qubit on a lattice graph $G$. Syndrome measurements define the graph structure, and the error propagation is governed by discrete exterior calculus principles.
key_observables: The primary observable is the topological scalar $\Delta J$, calculated as the difference in currents drained at two designated boundary sinks ($J_{	ext{in}}(v^{(1)}_b) - J_{	ext{in}}(v^{(2)}_b)$).
important_parameters: Code distance $d$ (e.g., $d=5, 7$), noise probability $p$, and the learned metric weights $w$.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that placing sinks on both boundaries allows for the isolation of a separating harmonic function ($\chi$) which defines the logical pairing, a structure lost with single-sink readouts.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the rotated surface code structure and the graph setup comparing single-sink versus two-sink architectures. The figures also schematically show current flow satisfying Kirchhoff's law and confirm that the topological pairing calculation matches the sink current difference.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the GNN decoder framework, details the use of Discrete Exterior Calculus to enforce physical constraints (Poisson equation), derives the key readout as a boundary-dependent topological pairing ($\Delta J$), validates this readout against full-field methods on increasing code distances, and discusses convergence analysis.
why_interesting: This work provides a mathematically rigorous and physically motivated alternative to standard decoding algorithms by grounding the error measurement in fundamental concepts of topology and differential forms (DEC).

FIG. 5. Pipeline of the physics-informed GNN decoder. The GINE encoder (L = 4 message-passing layers, hidden dimension 64) maps the input syndrome graph G to syndrome-adaptive edge embeddings, which an MLP converts to positive edge weights we. A Jacobi solver (KJ = 25 iterations) solves the discrete Poisson equation L(w)ϕ = ρ, yielding the node potentials ϕ and the edge-current vector Je = we(Bϕ)e, which satisfies the discrete Gauss law B⊤J = ρ exactly. A readout (Sec. III G) reduces ϕ or J to a scalar, and a classifier MLP maps it to a logical-error probability ˆy ∈[0, 1]. The output panel illustrates schematic edge currents: arrow thickness is proportional to |Je|.
